root.note: The TLFi explains English tennis as an altered form of this imperative, called out by the player who served. Early English forms such as tenetz (c. 1400) support it.

stages.meaning: the game of jeu de paume

history: Tennis is a French word that came home in English clothes. In the jeu de paume, the old indoor ball game, the player who served the ball called out to the other one: the TLFi explains English tennis as an altered form of tenez !, ‘take it!’, the polite imperative of tenir. Early English forms such as tenetz, around 1400, show the French behind it. In 1874 English named a new outdoor game lawn tennis, ‘tennis on grass’. French borrowed it back as lawn-tennis in 1877, and as plain tennis in 1880. So a French word left home as a shout and came back as a sport. In France des tennis are also trainers, the shoes.
historyEinfach: Tennis comes from French tenez!, ‘take it!’. Players of an old French ball game called this when they hit the ball. English took the word and made it tennis. Later the English game came to France, and French took the word back. Des tennis are also sports shoes.

elsewhere.text: A round trip: French gave English the word, English gave French the modern game and its name.
